papers.title: STCRank: Spatio-temporal Collaborative Ranking for Interactive Recommender System at Kuaishou E-shop
papers.authors: Boyang Xia, Ruilin Bao, Hanjun Jiang, Jun Wang, Wenwu Ou
papers.abstract: As a popular e-commerce platform, Kuaishou E-shop provides precise personalized product recommendations to tens of millions of users every day. To better respond real-time user feedback, we have deployed an interactive recommender system (IRS) alongside our core homepage recommender system. This IRS \footnotemark is triggered by user click on homepage, and generates a series of highly relevant recommendations based on the clicked item to meet focused browsing demands. Different from traditional e-commerce RecSys, the full-screen UI and immersive swiping down functionality present two distinct challenges for regular ranking system. First, there exists explicit interference (overlap or conflicts) between ranking objectives, i.e., conversion, view and swipe down. This is because there are intrinsic behavioral co-occurrences under the premise of immersive browsing and swiping down functionality. Second, the ranking system is prone to temporal greedy traps in sequential recommendation slot transitions, which is caused by full-screen UI design. To alleviate these challenges, we propose a novel Spatio-temporal collaborative ranking (STCRank) framework to achieve collaboration between multi-objectives within one slot (spatial) and between multiple sequential recommondation slots. In multi-objective collaboration (MOC) module, we push Pareto frontier by mitigating the objective overlaps and conflicts. In multi-slot collaboration (MSC) module, we achieve global optima on overall sequential slots by dual-stage look-ahead ranking mechanism. Extensive experiments demonstrate our proposed method brings about purchase and DAU co-growth. The proposed system has been already deployed at Kuaishou E-shop since 2025.6.

retrieval_meta.raw_source_name: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026

papers.summary: In a full-screen e-commerce feed where each swipe down brings the next item, the two ranking objectives of whether the user buys and whether they keep swiping fight each other. Kuaishou E-shop's data show that after a purchase, users leave right away without swiping 61.3% of the time. With the usual labels, every one of those purchases becomes a negative sample for the swipe objective, so the learned swipe score ends up pushing down the items that sell. The authors drop purchase-then-exit samples from the swipe negatives. Ranking also stops picking the top-scoring item one screen at a time. Instead it scores different orderings of the next few items: each item's value is multiplied by the probability that the user swipes far enough to reach it, and the ordering with the highest total wins. Adding this look-ahead ranking to the full-screen feed alone raised online purchases by 2.10%. Teams running immersive feeds should check their objectives for conflicting labels first.

papers.title: SAGE-PAIR: Source-Pretrained Routed Residual Adaptation for Sparse-Feedback Recommendation
papers.authors: Weiqing Zeng, Zida Yang, Guquan You, Jiexin Zheng, Cong Wang
papers.abstract: Recommendation systems often enter a new serving window before enough outcomes are available to retrain the deployed model. We study this regime with 0.05-1.0% target feedback, a range that spans our stress tests while keeping supervision far below the degrees of freedom of the source recommender. At this scale, existing fine-tuning and meta-learning methods still estimate target-specific updates from extremely sparse feedback, leaving the update direction weakly identified. SAGE-PAIR instead transfers a source-supported residual correction space and only calibrates this space using target outcomes. We introduce SAGE-PAIR, a staged adapter that pretrains a low-dimensional global residual on an adjacent source period and adds a soft router over residual experts conditioned on source user profiles. Target feedback then calibrates this residual state rather than relearning the recommender. On a locked test split of KuaiSAR-v2, SAGE-PAIR (Full) achieves a 1.77% relative improvement in NDCG
papers.note: 稀疏反馈排序适配；单数据集、代码可用
papers.summary: When a recommender moves into a new serving window, the target window often has too little feedback to retrain the live model. This paper freezes the original model and adds only a residual: the item features are click and like rates in the source window (exactly two dimensions), and the expert basis is a small set of anchors in that same plane. A soft router weights those anchors from the user's source-window behavior profile, and the extra term added to the original score is the inner product of the item features with that mixed direction. Scarce target feedback only updates these residual parameters. On a locked KuaiSAR-v2 test split, the full method raises NDCG@10 by 1.77% relative. Adding the routed experts gives a further 0.25% relative gain over source-pretrained residual adaptation without routing. When feedback is sparse, whether an update direction can be estimated may matter more than how many labels there are.

papers.title: Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control
papers.authors: Karina Romanova, Igor Kiselev, Vladimir Platonov, Viliana Devbunova, Gregory Leleytner, Adeliya Leleytner, Lina Veltman, Aleksandr Nikolich
papers.abstract: A common test of personalization replaces a user's history with someone else's and measures the drop in accuracy. But this swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may reflect topic mismatch. We examine this problem with a frozen language model on LaMP-2 news categorization, using histories from similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without history. Removing history only at evaluation makes this gain appear larger, at 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. With synthetic histories matched on labels and text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen during training and 0.65 points for unseen users, where the evidence for an advantage remains
papers.note: 个性化评估对照；多拆分与随机种子
papers.summary: A common personalization check replaces a user's own history with someone else's and watches accuracy drop. That swap also changes the topics in the history, so the drop may not mean the system recognized the person. On a frozen language model and LaMP-2 news classification, a user's own history beats using no history by 2.3 points. Keeping only each article's category label and dropping the text already reproduces 86% of the gap between own history and a random user's history. Synthetic histories are stitched from other users' articles that are closest in text to the target profile. When each slot must also match the category label at the same position in the original history, a user's own history beats this synthetic history by only 0.9 points. On unseen users, a user's own history beats similar-user histories by only 0.65 points, which is not yet strong evidence. Personalization tests should look at unseen users and compare against content-matched histories.

papers.title: What Matters for LLM Persona Simulation: Signal Form in Cold-Start E-Commerce Advertising
papers.authors: Jiwoo Choi, In Ik Lee, Woo Sung Seo, Minho Lee, Yun Young Choi
papers.abstract: Estimating advertising performance in cold-start settings is challenging because historical logs are unavailable before launch. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential alternative by simulating persona-conditioned user responses, but it remains unclear which design choices actually drive LLM-based persona simulation. Using real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic segments, we identify three signal-form dimensions that affect simulation quality: (i) a demographic anchor without noisy rich attributes, (ii) a relative qualitative banner-blindness signal rather than quantitative anchors, and (iii) prompt phrasing. On this campaign, our method attains an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1%, a 51.3% lower MAE than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM configuration using explicit CTR anchors. Systematic ablations show that minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, while relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors. We additionally compare these configurations with direct-prior and rule-based baselines and with alternative LLM configurations.
papers.summary: Before an ad campaign launches there are no historical logs, so cold-start performance is hard to estimate. When large language models simulate persona-conditioned user responses, what matters is which signals go into the prompt, not how richly the persona is written. On real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic groups, the method anchors on basic demographics without noisy extra attributes. The prompt notes that users often ignore banner ads even when the product seems relevant, instead of inserting numeric click-through rates. Mean absolute error between predicted and observed clicks across ad groups is 24.9 clicks. That is 51.3% lower than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM setup that uses explicit click-through-rate anchors. Minimal demographic descriptions also produce lower mean error than richer persona configurations.

papers.title: PAGSL: Path-Augmenting Graph Structure Learning for explainable scholar recommendation
papers.authors: Jiale Xu, Mingshu Ai, Junjie Huang, Tao Jia
papers.abstract: Explainable scholar recommendation aims to identify potential scholars of interest and provide reasonable explanations for the recommendations. However, existing frameworks struggle with optimization-induced noise and "hub node bias", yielding trivial explanations that lack hierarchical depth and personalization. To this end, we propose a novel explainable scholar recommendation model, Path-Augmenting Graph Structure Learning (named PAGSL). PAGSL combines representation learning and semantic path knowledge to ensure recommendation performance while providing interpretable results from two perspectives. Specifically, it activates latent academic paths among entities through graph augmentation and employs a path-based neural network to encode these paths for recommendation. A masking mechanism with path score optimization is designed to generate concise and informative explanations. We evaluate PAGSL on three academic datasets (Scholat, AMiner, and ResearchGate), comprising approximately
papers.note: 图路径推荐；三数据集与消融
papers.summary: Scholar recommendations often come with shallow, generic explanations, and highly connected nodes in the graph can pull those explanations off course. This work builds a subgraph for each scholar and that scholar's research attributes, adds type-specific edges between scholars who share an attribute, then extracts relational paths between a user and a candidate scholar for scoring. It masks lower-scoring paths so the remaining explanation is shorter and more informative. On the Scholat, AMiner, and ResearchGate academic datasets, recommendation F1 rises 6.31% and accuracy rises 6.29% over the strongest baseline. Ablations show that both heterogeneous convolution and path representation learning contribute to the gains.

papers.title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
papers.abstract: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.
papers.summary: Personalized explanations usually change their content or presentation. This study asks whether regularities in how users previously interpreted text can be used to reorder explanation sentences while leaving the wording fixed. In a within-participant study with 122 people, prior interpretations were summarized by what information they selected, what they treated as more salient, and how they organized relations. Sentences that matched the more salient, more often selected information in that profile were placed earlier. After reading sentences ordered by their own profile, participants answered 86.5% of objective comprehension questions correctly. The same sentences ordered by another person's profile scored 66.0%, and a language model that ordered them from the reader's own profile scored 73.0%. There was no reliable overall effect on whether people accepted the recommendation.
